title: Hit Time, Miss Penalty and the Average Access Time
unit: Memory Interfacing, Hierarchy and Cache Mapping
quickIdea: AMAT = hit time + miss rate x miss penalty. Every performance question in this topic is that one line, with the three quantities read off the question and the miss penalty sometimes itself a sum.
remember: Hit time is the time to deliver a word when it is in the cache - the tag compare plus the data read, and it is paid on every access, hits included.
Miss penalty is the extra time to bring the line from the next level down and load it; it is paid only on a miss.
Miss rate = 1 - hit ratio, and AMAT = hit time + (1 - hit ratio) x miss penalty.
A miss costs hit time + miss penalty on a hierarchical system, because the hit time was already spent before the miss was discovered.
Miss penalty is often itself a sum: the latency of the first word plus the transfer time for the rest of the block, which is why block size appears in performance questions.

example.prompt: GATE CSE 2020 Q.21: a 1 MB direct-mapped cache, 256 B blocks, 3 ns access time, 94% hit rate. On a miss the first word takes 20 ns and each further word 5 ns; the word is 64 bits. Find the AMAT.
example.work: A 256 B block holds 256/8 = 32 words of 64 bits. The miss penalty is 20 + 31 x 5 = 175 ns. AMAT = 0.94 x 3 + 0.06 x (3 + 175) = 2.82 + 10.68 = 13.5 ns.

gateAngle: The whole topic collapses into this formula, and GATE varies which of the three quantities is given. The two recurring traps are forgetting that a miss pays the hit time as well, and forgetting that the miss penalty covers the whole block rather than one word.

variations.label: VERIFIED PYQ
variations.question: GATE CSE 2020 Q.21, as worked above.
variations.why: The block is 32 words, so the transfer is 31 further words after the first: 20 + 31 x 5 = 175 ns, and the miss also pays the 3 ns hit time.

variations.label: PREDICTED VARIATION
variations.question: Same cache and memory, but the block size is doubled to 512 B. What is the AMAT?
variations.answer: 64 words per block, so the penalty is 20 + 63 x 5 = 335 ns and AMAT = 0.94 x 3 + 0.06 x 338 = 23.1 ns, if the hit rate does not change.
variations.why: It shows why block size cannot be raised without limit: the transfer time grows linearly with the block while the hit-rate gain saturates.

variations.label: CONCEPTUAL PRACTICE QUESTION
variations.question: A cache with a 2 ns hit time and a 0.5 hit ratio misses to memory taking 100 ns. By how much does a 1 ns faster hit time change the AMAT, and by how much does a 5-point better hit ratio?
variations.answer: AMAT is 2 + 0.5 x 100 = 52 ns. A 1 ns faster hit time gives 51 ns; a 0.55 hit ratio gives 2 + 0.45 x 100 = 47 ns.
variations.why: It shows which knob matters: when the miss rate is high, the miss term dominates and improving the hit time is nearly pointless.

trap.what: Computing AMAT as hit ratio x hit time + miss rate x miss penalty, which charges a miss only the penalty.
trap.why: On a hierarchical system the hit time is spent on a miss too, before the miss is detected; only a simultaneous-access system, which GATE must state explicitly, avoids it.
trap.counterexample: Hit time 3 ns, penalty 175 ns, 94% hits. The wrong form gives 0.94 x 3 + 0.06 x 175 = 13.32 ns; the right form gives 13.5 ns - and the two differ by exactly the miss rate times the hit time.

check.question: Hit time 2 ns, hit ratio 0.9, miss penalty 40 ns. What is the AMAT, and what would it be with a perfect cache?
check.answer: AMAT = 2 + 0.1 x 40 = 6 ns; with a perfect cache it is 2 ns, so the cache misses cost three times the hit time.
check.explanation: The perfect-cache figure is the hit time alone, which is the floor any AMAT can reach.
